answer.question: Which competitors were mentioned, and in what context?
answer.answer: Named competitors span Zapier, Workato, Power Automate, Tray.io, MuleSoft, Gainsight, Retool Workflows, Make and Guidewire; they appeared as incumbents, price anchors, active bake-offs, and winners or replacements in churn [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8]. Zapier was the most widespread: incumbent, price anchor, and replacement tool [1]. Workato and Tray.io were the most direct head-to-head rivals, and Workato won the Verity Payments deal [2][4]. Power Automate was a licensing-backed incumbent at four prospects or customers [3]. Some mentions were unnamed vendors or in-house workarounds [9].

claims.text: Zapier: Acme Logistics (Rachel Morgan) used it only as a mental price anchor; Maya Chen called it a common but wrong anchor. Cedar & Finch (Sophie Reed) pays about $200/month, likes it for simple work, and may keep it (Zapier plus better documentation) rather than over-buy; Leo Grant said OrbitFlow's edge is structural (about 60 Zaps vs about 8 subflows), not that Zapier can't do things. Fable Media (Imogen Price) has about 20 Zaps, says it does about 80% of what they need, and the founder will compare OrbitFlow's £21k to Zapier's about £2k; Alastair McCrae called it a toy and Imogen pushed back. Lumen Retail was a prior Zapier estate (about 60 Zaps, half orphaned) it moved away from. evidence.context: OrbitFlow staff position the product against generic iPaaS or internal-services integration: some customers keep those for deep systems integration and use OrbitFlow for business-owned workflows. — Generic category of alternative, not a named vendor. Vendor framed it as complementary, not a replacement.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: I spoke to a workflow vendor there and I cannot remember which one
evidence.context: An unnamed workflow vendor was met by the customer at Hannover Messe. The customer cannot recall which vendor it was. OrbitFlow staff say it was not them. — Unnamed competitor the customer cannot identify. No comparison made. Vendor denied it was OrbitFlow based on stand colour and stand presence.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: If you do that, you will be the second vendor this year who has.
evidence.context: Another, unnamed vendor this year provided transparent pricing in a proposal. The customer calls OrbitFlow the second such vendor and declined to name the first. — Implicit competitor comparison on pricing transparency. Customer refused to name the first vendor.

evidence.speaker: Ben Foster
evidence.quote: two other vendors we've spoken to had it as an enterprise-only feature
evidence.context: Prospect mentions other vendors they have spoken to; one had SSO as enterprise-only, and the prospect expects OrbitFlow may be similar. — Unnamed competing vendors in evaluation; used as a basis to question OrbitFlow's SSO claim.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: people compensate — they build their own reminders, their own little spreadsheets, someone wrote a script once.
evidence.context: Internal workarounds (personal reminders, spreadsheets, custom scripts) act as an informal alternative currently in use. — Generic alternative: the status quo of homegrown tooling that the prospect says is fragile and person-dependent. Three unowned scripts were reported.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Replacing several departmental Python scripts with centrally visible automations and approvals.
evidence.context: Departmental unofficial scripts are an existing in-house workaround. DeltaWorks has identified 31 that it knows of and believes there are more. The customer wants them replaced with centrally visible automations. — Home-built alternative that the customer is trying to replace in a possible second phase. Count is approximate, from a non-exhaustive audit.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: they create unofficial scripts to work around it
evidence.context: Local teams build unofficial scripts to work around failed or silent automations. Central IT cannot govern them because it does not know they exist. — Describes the status quo workaround. Anika gave a specific example: a script that ran for four years using an over-privileged service account.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: It's also "keep the scripts and document them better." That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
evidence.context: Prospect states a non-vendor alternative: keep the existing scripts and document them better. The prospect expects this to be proposed internally. — Generic alternative (status quo with documentation), considered cheaper; not a product.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: High-value operational exceptions are currently handled through Slack channels and custom scripts.
evidence.context: Prospect's current process is handled through Slack and custom scripts, which is the incumbent alternative. — Incumbent, built in-house rather than a vendor product.

conflicts.description: Alastair McCrae at Fable Media dismissed Zapier as a toy, while Imogen Price said it does about 80% of what they need. Maya Chen at Acme and Leo Grant at Cedar & Finch instead framed Zapier as a wrong anchor or a structural-maintenance comparison.

conflicts.topic: Whether to claim superiority over incumbents
conflicts.description: Reps differed in tone: Leo Grant said OrbitFlow both loses to and beats Tray and told Kestrel Robotics to run the test against Tray, while Maya Chen said OrbitFlow cannot beat Power Automate's bundled licensing on price.

not_covered: Whether any competitor was actually named in the unnamed vendor mentions at DeltaWorks, Fable Media or Juniper Cloud Tools.
Outcomes of the open competitive evaluations (Ember Financial vs Tray, Kestrel Robotics vs Tray, Greenline's Power Automate benchmark).
assumptions: Question is about all sales calls in the corpus, so no call type filter applied.
Competitor list in search terms is illustrative; the reader should capture any named vendor found in the transcript.
The competitor list was treated as any named vendor or tool, including incumbent tools and in-house alternatives, per the stated assumptions.

grades.reason: Citation [6] states Oakhill paid £1,800/month for 30 users with 4 logging in, and says a plan at £500-600/month would have kept them and no smaller plan exists. Answer text itself says only 'no smaller tier' but the quoted evidence covers the specifics.
Pricing concerns are cited from many companies, including Acme, Cedar & Finch, Fable Media, Trafford Dental, Ember and others.

answer.question: What concerns did customers raise about pricing?
answer.answer: The most common were that the headline price (Growth at $1,800/month) was above expectations or unaffordable, and fear of paying full seats for occasional approvers [1][2]. Others were hidden or usage-based charges, ROI and value justification versus cheaper alternatives, and approval-threshold and budget constraints [3][4][5]. Churned customers cited paying for unused capacity and no smaller tier [6]. Some customers said base price was not the concern [7].

claims.text: Several prospects said Growth at $1,800/month was too high or above expectations: Acme Logistics (Rachel Morgan, benchmarked against Zapier), Cedar & Finch (Sophie Reed expected about 800-1,000), and Fable Media (Imogen Price, 'above what I had in mind'). Trafford Dental Group's Yvonne Deeks called it 'not a number that exists in my world', named £200-300/month as her budget, and said price would have meant a no regardless of pitch (one finding on the decisive outcome is inferred).

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: It's more than I expected. And I know why — I'd mentally benchmarked this against Zapier, which is not a fair comparison, but that's the number that was in my head.
evidence.context: Customer says Growth pricing ($1,800/month) is more than expected, anchored on Zapier as a benchmark, which they admit is not a fair comparison. — Deferred: OrbitFlow said it would return to pricing once the user model is known (T041), so the concern is not resolved on this call.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
evidence.context: Sophie Reed said Growth's £/$1,800 per month price is hard for a team their size; she had expected roughly 800-1,000 per month, and the gap is left open. — Core pricing objection. Vendor acknowledged the gap but did not close it. Left open.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: That's above what I had in mind.
evidence.context: Customer said the Growth package price of eighteen hundred a month was above what she had in mind. — Initial price reaction to Growth package; left open, no resolution on price in the call.

evidence.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
evidence.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is not a number that exists in my world.
evidence.context: Customer said OrbitFlow's entry package at £1,800/month is not affordable; the price is the real problem and not a number that exists in her world. — Price objection raised directly after vendor quoted entry package; left open-ended but effectively a no. Customer stressed it is the real problem even if the pitch had been better.

evidence.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
evidence.quote: For something like this? Two, three hundred a month, and I'd have to justify it.
evidence.context: Customer stated her acceptable budget for this type of product is two to three hundred pounds a month, and she would have to justify even that. — Given when asked what number would work; far below the £1,800 entry price. Vendor concluded 'then we're not it' and customer agreed.

evidence.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
evidence.quote: you'd still probably have got a no because of the price.
evidence.context: Customer said price would likely have ended the deal regardless of pitch quality, so the call ended as a no on price. — Customer's reasoning on the outcome; she also said a better opener would have made the call less annoying but price still drives the no.

evidence.speaker: Yvonne Deeks
evidence.quote: You're not it.
evidence.context: Customer's price concern appears decisive: the call's outcome is a no driven by budget, not product fit. — Inference from the customer's repeated price statements and the vendor's conclusion 'then we're not it'.

claims.text: Per-seat licensing for occasional approvers was a recurring concern. Acme Logistics, BrightPath Health, DeltaWorks Manufacturing (Anika Bose), Ember Financial (Noah Williams, plus Hannah Cole saying users may exceed 300), Greenline Energy Services (Carlos Mendes: 'over before it starts'), Harbor Legal (Samir Khan and Eleanor Brooks) and Inkwell Learning (Olivia Grant, 62 CSMs) did not want to find out later that approvers need full seats. Fable Media's Imogen Price objected to paying for 30 seats when she needed 10. Vendors generally agreed to itemise in the proposal but gave no numbers.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: Please make that explicit in the proposal. I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
evidence.context: Customer does not want to discover mid-contract that occasional approvers need full paid seats; wants seat requirements explicit in the proposal. — Open pricing-model concern. OrbitFlow agreed to itemise builder and viewer/approver counts but did not give a number (T135, T137).

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: Yes, because we may have a small number of builders and a lot of people who only approve something or receive a notification.
evidence.context: Customer's team may have few builders but many approval-only or notification-only users, so per-seat cost depends on how users are categorised. — Deferred: OrbitFlow said approval-only users can be structured differently by package but gave no figures.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: What counts as a user?
evidence.context: Customer asks what counts as a licensed user, since they expect a few builders and many occasional approvers or notification recipients. — Raised as a pricing-model question. Maya said builders and full workspace users are licensed, and approval-only or notification-only users may be structured differently. Maya declined to quote a figure until the user model is known. Status: open.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: I don't want to discover in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
evidence.context: Customer does not want to discover later that every occasional approver needs a full seat, and wants the seat model explicit in the proposal. — Cost-surprise concern. Maya committed to an itemised proposal covering assumed builders, viewers, approvers, expected volume and one-time services. Status: deferred to the proposal, with a commitment from the vendor.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: We may have twenty people building and several hundred who only approve something.
evidence.context: Customer wants explicit pricing for occasional approvers and fears paying full seats for them in year two; vendor said it would be explicit but gave no number. — Seat cost concern; deferred pending user model and architecture review.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: Please put that in the proposal explicitly. I do not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver requires a full seat.
evidence.context: Customer does not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver needs a full seat. — Explicit concern about per-seat cost scaling; vendor committed to make it explicit.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Make that split explicit in the proposal. I don't want to find out in year two that every approver needs a full seat.
evidence.context: Customer wants per-user licensing split explicit so approver-only users do not require full seats; concern about year-two cost. — Licensing concern about seat counts for 40 builders and up to 300 approvers/viewers; vendor agreed to itemise. Deferred to proposal.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Three hundred is optimistic, by the way. It might be more.
evidence.context: Customer noted user count may grow beyond 300, raising cost exposure; vendor agreed to model 300 and 500 users. — Seat-count growth concern; vendor to model scenarios. Deferred.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
evidence.context: Customer objects that supervisors would need full seats, which would make the deal unviable; concern left open pending a builder vs approver breakdown. — Licensing model concern. Vendor said approval-only populations can be structured differently, but gave no number.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Six builders, several hundred approvers.
evidence.context: Customer states the population sizes: about six builders and several hundred approvers, which bears on licensing cost. — Customer supplied the counts so vendor could structure pricing; vendor said the shape must be explicit in writing before any internal take-forward.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: What's a user? We'd have very few builders and a very large number of partners who approve something occasionally.
evidence.context: Samir Khan asks how a user is defined, expecting few builders but many partners who approve only occasionally, which affects licence cost. — Per-seat licensing question. Vendor declined to give a number until the licensed-user split is known, saying a number would be misleading. Deferred.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: Please put the split in writing when you do. If it turns out every partner needs a seat, this is a very short conversation.
evidence.context: Eleanor Brooks asks for the seat split in writing, warning that if every partner needs a seat the deal becomes a very short conversation. — Seat-cost sensitivity. Vendor committed to providing the split in writing. Deferred pending that document.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: I don't want to find out in month four that all sixty-two need full seats.
evidence.context: Customer wants pricing made explicit by user split so seat costs are not a surprise later, for builders versus the roughly sixty-two task-receiving CSMs. — Concern about per-seat licensing exposure; Maya deferred any figure until the itemised proposal, so it is deferred.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: So I'd be paying for twenty seats I don't need.
evidence.context: Customer objected to paying for thirty seats when she needed ten, saying she would be paying for twenty seats she does not need. — Seat-count objection; vendor said the thirty-user package price is fixed. Not resolved.

claims.text: Customers worried about hidden, usage-based or scaling costs. Ember Financial's Noah Williams raised overage unpredictability and asked 'Can you cap it?' (vendor declined to promise a cap). Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed was wary of surprise costs from AI or usage pricing. DeltaWorks' Martin Vogel wanted transparency on services and premium connectors. Acme and BrightPath required a model without hidden scaling surprises. Juniper Cloud Tools' Ava Sinclair and Marcus Chen worried about per-event or per-run billing, and Marcus asked for the pricing model in writing (vendor committed to week two). Lumen Retail's Fiona Bright said the run tier was wrong after overages, and asked for changes shown separately for her finance director.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Usage overages. If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine.
evidence.context: Customer raised concern about unpredictable usage overage charges growing the bill over time; vendor deferred specifics until modelling volumes, with overage mechanism to be put explicitly in contract (left open pending modelling). — Noah raised the pricing concern about second-year invoices; vendor committed to modelling and contract terms but gave no specific cap. Open.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Can you cap it?
evidence.context: Customer asked whether usage could be capped; vendor declined to promise a cap before modelling volumes. Left open. — Direct pricing question about a cap; vendor avoided committing on the call.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Everyone says that and then there's a surprise later.
evidence.context: Sophie Reed asked whether the AI features or usage-based pricing would cost extra; Leo said usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connectors and would be modelled. Customer is wary of surprise costs. Deferred. — Hidden-fee concern about usage pricing.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software. What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review.
evidence.context: Customer says the headline licence price will not surprise him, but he cares about transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and costs only discovered after architecture review; deferred to proposal transparency commitment. — Pricing concern raised by customer; vendor committed to itemised proposal, so partially addressed but open until the proposal arrives.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
evidence.context: Customer requires a commercial model without hidden scaling surprises as a condition for moving from evaluation to decision. — Stated decision criterion; not resolved on the call.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: A commercial model without hidden scaling surprises.
evidence.context: Customer wants a commercial model without hidden scaling surprises as a condition for a decision. — Stated among criteria for moving from evaluation to a decision. Status: open.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: What I do not want is to pay you per event.
evidence.context: Customer (Ava Sinclair) raised concern that per-event pricing would make high-volume event processing too expensive; left open pending vendor confirmation of pricing unit. — Cost concern about paying per event; vendor said filter upstream so only business events reach OrbitFlow. Customer's concern not fully resolved, she still asked about the pricing unit.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: If I emit a business event and it triggers a workflow that fans out to five subflows, is that one run or six?
evidence.context: Customer (Ava Sinclair) worried that subflow invocations may each be billed as separate runs, which would make the recommended composition pattern expensive; deferred to written billing answer. — Vendor (Nina Patel) said subflow invocations are believed to be counted but could not confirm billing semantics; deferred to written answer due by Friday.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: My question is whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic compared with keeping the event-handling layer in AWS.
evidence.context: Customer (Marcus Chen) asked whether usage limits make high-volume event processing uneconomic versus keeping the event layer in AWS; he suggested it may answer itself. — Economics question about usage limits; partly answered by vendor saying it depends on what counts as a run; left open.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: That's what happened with our observability vendor.
evidence.context: Customer (Marcus Chen) said the prior observability vendor's pricing had caused cost problems twice; the bill was a trigger for dropping the tool. — Background on past vendor cost experience shaping the buyer's sensitivity to usage-based invoices.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: I'd like the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends, not after. If the economics don't work I'd rather know in week three.
evidence.context: Customer (Marcus Chen) asked for the pricing model in writing before the evaluation ends, so economics can be known by week three; vendor committed to week two. — Commercial concern about ROI/economics; resolved as a commitment, to be delivered in week two.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: But it does mean the run tier is wrong.
evidence.context: Customer said the run tier is wrong because of the overages, which the vendor agreed with. — Run-tier sizing concern raised after overage discussion; vendor said the tier change is the main thing to discuss, so this was deferred to the renewal proposal.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: I have to take it to a finance director who will ask what changed and why.
evidence.context: Customer asked for the two changes (seat reduction and run-tier increase) shown separately because a finance director will ask what changed and why. — Budget justification requirement; vendor agreed to show last year's and next year's line items side by side. Deferred to the Friday proposal.

claims.text: Customers questioned ROI and value versus cheaper alternatives. Fable Media's Imogen Price asked what $21k buys over Zapier at $2k, and said Zapier plus process discipline may suffice. Acme Logistics wanted a clearer ROI story and was weighing a Workato expansion. Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed was not convinced value closes the gap. Greenline said Power Automate's favourable licensing matters. BrightPath cited its Microsoft agreement covering Power Automate. Harbor Legal's Samir Khan feared disproportionate integration spend. Inkwell Learning challenged the retention ROI, and Lumen's Fiona Bright questioned 9% more cost for 40% more capacity. Pinewood Insurance's Graham Attwood said they pay for Enterprise and get very little.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: he'll ask what we get for twenty-one thousand that we don't get from Zapier for two thousand, and I need a better answer than "it's more robust."
evidence.context: Customer questioned the return on investment versus Zapier, asking what the company gets for twenty-one thousand that it does not get from Zapier for two thousand. — ROI/value concern raised for founder approval; vendor answered with governance and audit trail, which customer rejected as irrelevant to an agency. Left open.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: Price and complexity are the two risks. And honestly, we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough
evidence.context: Customer said Zapier plus better process discipline may be good enough, so price and complexity are real risks to the deal. — Price-driven alternative; customer said she is interested but not dismissing it. Open.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I can probably still justify it if we replace enough manual work, and maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for. But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
evidence.context: Customer can justify the price only if the platform replaces enough manual work and some Gainsight spend, and needs a clearer ROI story than time savings. — Open: OrbitFlow proposed baselining elapsed time, manual touches, exception rate and engineer hours for a pilot (T142), but no ROI case was agreed on the call.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor. That's the conversation I'll have to win internally.
evidence.context: Customer says the real commercial question is whether to expand the existing Workato contract rather than add another vendor, and this is the internal battle they must win. — Open: OrbitFlow agreed to write it as a pilot exit criterion (T129). Tom also named Workato or improving the status quo as the honest comparison (T153).

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
evidence.context: Sophie Reed said she likes the monitoring and templates but is not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools they already pay for. Left open. — Final stance on value versus cost. Customer is not saying no.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: And we get favourable licensing on it, which matters more than I'd like it to.
evidence.context: Customer says Power Automate's favourable licensing matters, and that the comparison is partly about cost. Vendor conceded it cannot beat bundled licensing on price; the customer's internal case must be operational cost rather than licence cost. — Cost comparison against incumbent. Deferred to operational-cost argument; the customer's own internal case is still to be built.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: It's already covered by our Microsoft agreement, which matters a lot to procurement.
evidence.context: Power Automate is already covered by the customer's Microsoft agreement, which matters to procurement, so an alternative that replaces it on cost grounds is a real comparison. — Licensing/cost context from the customer. Maya said a proposal to migrate everything off Microsoft would lose to the licensing agreement, and Priya agreed.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: We end up spending a great deal to automate something that saves a business services person four hours a week.
evidence.context: Samir Khan says the integration effort may be disproportionate to the value, since automating the process saves only about four hours a week of business services time. This is his stated biggest risk and is left open pending the integration assessment and services estimate. — Customer ROI concern about cost versus value. Vendor (Leo Grant) responded that the test is an operation-by-operation difficulty assessment plus a services estimate, to be compared against the cost of delayed matter opening. Left open.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: It relies on the counterfactual. We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
evidence.context: Customer challenged the ROI case, saying renewal-retention benefit depends on a counterfactual that cannot be proven. — ROI objection; Maya responded by proposing a leading indicator (time from first signal to first intervention), which Darren found a better framing. Partly resolved, but the renewal ROI claim remains unproven.

evidence.speaker: Fiona Bright
evidence.quote: Nine percent for forty percent more capacity and a new use case.
evidence.context: Customer questioned whether the total spend is justified: nine percent more cost for forty percent more capacity plus a new use case. — Value/ROI concern about the renewal total; vendor said the seat reduction is real and not offset by an inflated run tier. Left open pending the proposal.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: that we're paying for Enterprise and getting very little
evidence.context: Customer states they are paying for Enterprise while getting very little value from it. — Customer agrees with the vendor's ROI view; deferred to the renewal decision.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: That's precisely the position I'm in.
evidence.context: Customer says the product is 'a very expensive product that nobody operates' when only one builder is active; Graham agrees he is in that position. — Cost/value concern raised by vendor's hypothetical, accepted by customer; left open (not resolved, tied to enablement plan).

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Is Enterprise worth it for what you're getting', and right now the honest answer is probably not, because you're getting very little.
evidence.context: Customer questions whether Enterprise tier is worth the cost given minimal usage of its features; vendor agrees it probably is not. — Return-on-investment concern on tier spend; vendor proposed Growth tier, customer's security requirement (SSO) makes Growth unviable, so left open with a six-month option proposed.

claims.text: Budget approval thresholds created friction: Acme's finance gets involved above $25k/year, Fable Media's Imogen Price can sign up to £20k (the proposal is about £21.5k), and Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed can approve under 15,000 while Growth (21,600/year) goes to the COO and finance director. Fable Media also asked for monthly billing or starting with 10 users, which was left to manager approval. Cedar & Finch's Sophie Reed asked about annual prepay, and the vendor said the discount is meaningful but not a halving. Pinewood's Graham Attwood asked about a six-month discount, and the vendor said no discount, only pro-rata.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: Finance gets involved above twenty-five thousand a year, so — yes, finance gets involved.
evidence.context: Purchases above $25,000 a year trigger finance involvement at the customer. — Budget-approval threshold stated by customer, relevant to deal size and approval path.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
evidence.context: Customer stated her spending authority is capped at twenty thousand; anything above requires founder approval, and the proposed annual cost exceeds that. — Budget constraint; Ben computed the annual figure as twenty-one and a half thousand. Left open.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership.
evidence.context: Sophie Reed said budget is the biggest risk and that the team may decide it is over-buying and keep Zapier; she also said she can approve tools under 15,000 a year alone, and the Growth price (21,600 a year) goes to the COO and finance director. — Approval threshold and budget risk. Left open; slower process above threshold.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: Is there any way to start with ten users? Or bill monthly while we prove the process before committing for a year?
evidence.context: Customer asked whether she could start with ten users or bill monthly to prove the process before committing to an annual contract. — Customer sought lower-commitment pricing; vendor said monthly was 'usually fine' but needed manager approval, so left open and deferred.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: can you confirm the monthly billing thing properly rather than "probably"? Because if that's not actually available I'd rather know now.
evidence.context: Customer wants vendor to confirm monthly billing explicitly, saying she would rather know now if it is unavailable. — Pricing term not confirmed; vendor said he would check with his manager. Deferred.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: I could potentially do an annual prepay if that materially changes the number. Does it?
evidence.context: Sophie Reed asked whether an annual prepay would materially change the price; Leo said it gives a meaningful discount but not a halving. Deferred/left open. — Customer probed discount options; vendor said discount is modest.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: Would you discount six months?
evidence.context: Customer asks whether the vendor will discount a six-month term; vendor says no discount and no short-term premium, only pro-rata at the annual rate. — Discount/pricing question on the short renewal option; resolved by vendor offer (no uplift, no penalty).

claims.text: Churned customers cited poor value for money. Oakhill Property's Hazel Wren said they paid £1,800/month for 30 users with 4 logging in, that £19k was not worth it, and that Zapier at about £2,000/year was cheaper. She refused a discount, and said a plan at £500-600/month would have kept them (with approval forms), but no smaller plan exists. Verity Payments' Kwame Boateng and Sarah Lindqvist said the premium was not worth it and the licence cost went unjustified (about $100k/year). Kwame said Workato was only somewhat cheaper, so price was partly but not primarily the reason for switching.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: We were on Growth, at eighteen hundred a month, for thirty users, when we had four people who ever logged in.
evidence.context: Customer says Growth plan at £1,800/month for 30 seats was far more than they needed, since only four people logged in, so they were paying for capacity they never used. — Core pricing/ROI complaint; cost mismatch between seats and actual use. Unresolved: the account is churning.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: nineteen thousand pounds is a member of staff for four months
evidence.context: Customer says the product's value to them is not worth the annual price, and frames the cost as a staff salary. — Main reason for churn; the customer does not dispute product quality. Left open: the vendor did not offer a lower price that changed the decision.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: About two thousand a year. Maybe two and a half with the tier we need.
evidence.context: Customer says the replacement tool, Zapier, costs about £2,000 a year, roughly a tenth of OrbitFlow's price, and they are switching for cost reasons. — Cost comparison behind the churn decision. The customer accepts losing some features for the saving.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: If you can do it for eight thousand now, that tells me you could have done it for eight thousand two years ago, and then I'd be quite cross.
evidence.context: Customer rejected a discount offer from the AE, saying a lower price now would show they had been overcharged earlier. — Vendor (Alastair) offered to look at pricing; customer refused. Resolved by refusal: no discount was agreed, and the customer stayed on the decision to leave.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer and I'd probably have done the compliance one eventually.
evidence.context: Customer says a smaller, cheaper plan would have kept them as a customer, but no such tier exists. — Pricing-structure concern; the vendor confirmed there is no smaller plan and the entry point is Growth. Left open/deferred: the vendor only said it would pass the feedback on.

evidence.speaker: Hazel Wren
evidence.quote: With the approval forms, yes. Without them, no, because that's the bit Zapier can't do and it's the only thing I'll actually miss.
evidence.context: Customer says a plan around £500/month would only win them back if it included approval forms, which were the feature they valued most. — Conditional interest in a lower-priced tier; the customer will not buy it without approval forms.
