evidence.context: Prospect called the price above what she had in mind and said pricing will decide the deal. — Price objection raised directly after the OrbitFlow price was stated.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
evidence.context: Prospect states a budget constraint: she can sign software contracts up to £20,000 a year, above which the founder must approve; OrbitFlow's Growth package is £1,800/month (about £21,500/year). — Pricing exceeds her signing authority, creating a required approval step with the founder.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: So I'd be paying for twenty seats I don't need.
evidence.context: Prospect objects to paying for 20 unneeded seats on the 30-user package. — Per-seat objection; vendor deflected to 'paying for the platform'.

claims.text: Greenline Energy Services: Carlos Mendes says it is exploration, not procurement, and a decision would fall in the budget cycle starting in October. The Microsoft platform team will resist, there is a first-class Dynamics gap, and a seat model requiring supervisors would end the evaluation. Near-term likelihood appears low (inferred).

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: I want to be honest that it's exploration, not a procurement process.
evidence.context: Customer states the decision is exploration, not a procurement process, and no decision is realistic this year. — Stated timing and intent; undercuts near-term purchase likelihood.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Budgeting for next fiscal year starts in October, so if anything were to happen it'd be in that cycle.
evidence.context: Customer says a decision would fall in the next budget cycle, with budgeting for next fiscal year starting in October. — Stated timeline for a possible decision; conditional on roadmap and architecture conversation.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The Microsoft platform team will not want this. Not because it's bad. Because it isn't Microsoft.
evidence.context: Customer says the Microsoft platform team will not want this and has killed things before; influence is formal but practical impact depends on objection strength. — Named blocker/influencer in decision process.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us. Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it.
evidence.context: Customer says the first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue and OrbitFlow must be materially better to displace the embedded, approved Power Automate. — Objection/blocker to purchase; the incumbent is licensed, approved and liked by the platform team.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
evidence.context: Licensing model is a major concern: customer has hundreds of supervisors who should not need full seats, and says a seat model requiring them would end the evaluation. — Per-seat pricing objection; OrbitFlow declined to give a number.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Realistically, no.
evidence.context: Inferred: overall purchase likelihood in the near term is low; the customer is interested but early, with the main blockers being the Microsoft platform team, incumbent licensing, and the lack of a first-class Dynamics connector. — Synthesis of stated objections and timing; not a customer statement.

conflicts.description: Carlos is open to a benchmark pilot and the price may be defensible, yet says it is exploration and realistically no near-term decision.
The sponsor is broadly positive and wants to move, but Hannah Cole describes Tray as having a six-week head start and a cheaper alternative could be proposed.

not_covered: No actual purchase outcomes or probabilities are in the findings; this is a judgement from signals only.
assumptions: 'Prospects' interpreted as calls of type Prospect (new business), excluding renewals, churned customers and cold calls.
Likelihood to purchase is a judgement across calls, so each call is read for underlying buying signals rather than a ranking.
Prospects means calls of type Prospect only, excluding renewals, churned customers and cold calls.
Likelihood is a judgement from buying signals, not a ranking from the data.

grades.reason: Answer covers price vs budget: Cedar & Finch $800-1,000 vs $1,800/month, and Fable Media's above-£20k founder approval/signing limit with price as deciding factor.
Answer names Workato at Acme, Power Automate at Greenline, and in-house builds at Juniper as alternatives.
Answer cites BrightPath's BAA gate, Harbor Legal's UK residency and ethical walls, and written assurances, plus DeltaWorks' 240-question security questionnaire.
Answer frames themes as recurring across all 10 prospect calls and cites well over four different prospects (Acme, BrightPath, Cedar & Finch, Fable, Greenline, etc.).

answer.question: What are the most common reasons prospects hesitate to buy?
answer.answer: Across all 10 Prospect calls, the most recurring hesitations were pricing and licensing, especially per-seat surprises [1][2]. Security, compliance and data-residency gates also recurred, including written no-training commitments and AI exclusion from phase one [3][4]. Prospects also named status quo or existing tools as the real alternative and raised internal approval and timing hurdles [5][6]. Integration and architecture fit and maintenance or adoption risk came up as well [7][8].

claims.text: Price level and ROI justification were raised in many calls. Acme Logistics said price was above expectation and wanted a clearer ROI story. Cedar & Finch expected $800-1,000 versus $1,800/month. Fable Media's Imogen Price called price the deciding factor, said she would pay for about 20 unneeded seats, and wanted monthly billing. Greenline said Power Automate wins on cost per seat. Juniper does not want to pay per event.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: It's more than I expected. And I know why — I'd mentally benchmarked this against Zapier, which is not a fair comparison
evidence.context: Pricing was higher than the prospect expected, anchored on Zapier as a benchmark. — Customer framed it as more than expected; acknowledged the Zapier comparison is unfair but still the number in her head. Vendor responded by deferring a number until user model is known.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
evidence.context: Prospect could justify the price only with a clearer ROI story than time savings, and may need to offset Gainsight spend. — Customer conditional on replacing enough manual work and possibly retiring Gainsight; vendor deferred pricing discussion.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
evidence.context: Prospect finds Growth price ($1,800/month) hard for a team their size; expected closer to $800-1,000. — Pricing objection raised by Sophie; Leo acknowledged the gap but did not dispute it.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: Let's talk about money, because that's going to decide this.
evidence.context: Prospect's main hesitation is price: the Growth package at £1,800/month is above what she had in mind. — Pricing objection raised after vendor quoted Growth package; prospect framed it as the deciding factor.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: So I'd be paying for twenty seats I don't need.
evidence.context: Prospect is hesitant to pay for thirty seats when she needs about ten; she sees paying for unused seats as a cost problem. — Per-seat/package mismatch; vendor said the thirty-user package price is fixed.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: Or bill monthly while we prove the process before committing for a year?
evidence.context: Annual commitment is a barrier; prospect wants monthly billing to prove the process first. Vendor's monthly availability was unconfirmed. — Prospect asked for monthly billing as a lower-risk trial; vendor said 'usually fine' and needed manager approval.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: If the decision is purely cost per seat, Microsoft wins and everyone knows it.
evidence.context: Cost objection: Power Automate's bundled favourable licensing makes OrbitFlow hard to justify on cost per seat; the case must rest on operational cost instead — Maya conceded Microsoft wins on pure licence cost; Carlos accepted this is the argument he would need to make internally; Maya proposed measuring the support time as a number

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: What I do not want is to pay you per event.
evidence.context: Prospect's main hesitation is that usage-based pricing on high-volume event processing could make the product uneconomic versus keeping event handling in AWS; she does not want to pay per event. — Cost/pricing objection raised early, then tied to volume; OrbitFlow staff responded by recommending filtering upstream and said the design avoids per-event cost.

claims.text: Per-seat licensing surprises for occasional approvers were raised independently at Acme Logistics, BrightPath Health, DeltaWorks, Greenline, Harbor Legal and Inkwell, and at Greenline and Harbor they were deal-ending ('over before it starts', 'very short conversation'). Hidden usage, overage and services costs worried Cedar & Finch, DeltaWorks, Ember and Juniper (subflow billing).

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
evidence.context: Concern about per-seat surprises: wants explicit treatment of occasional approvers versus full seats. — Customer worried about month-four surprise; vendor said pricing will be itemised and approval-only users may be structured differently.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: I don't want to discover in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
evidence.context: Prospect is wary of per-seat licensing surprises, especially for occasional approvers and notification-only users. — Vendor declined to quote a figure until a user model is built; said builders and full users are licensed and approvers can be structured differently.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: I do not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver requires a full seat.
evidence.context: Prospect is concerned about per-seat pricing ambiguity; wants explicit treatment of occasional approvers to avoid unexpected cost in year two. — OrbitFlow declines to give a number until the user model is known and commits to a separated, explicit proposal.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
evidence.context: Per-seat licensing model could kill the deal: supervisors and approvers should not need full seats — Raised as a licensing concern; approver population (hundreds) versus builders (about six) was not yet priced; Maya declined to give a number without those counts

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: If it turns out every partner needs a seat, this is a very short conversation.
evidence.context: Licensing per user is a concern. If partners each need a seat, the deal becomes unviable. — Samir asked what counts as a user. Leo declined to give a number until the licence split between builders and approval-only users was clear.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: I don't want to find out in month four that all sixty-two need full seats.
evidence.context: Concern that per-seat licensing could be much higher than expected if all CSM task recipients need full seats. — About 60-62 CSMs receive tasks versus 3-4 builders. Maya said the split would be itemised in the proposal and no figure was quoted on the call.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Everyone says that and then there's a surprise later.
evidence.context: Prospect is wary of hidden usage-based costs for AI features and premium connectors. — Pricing-surprise concern raised about AI digest; vendor offered to model assumptions in writing.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review. That is where the surprises live.
evidence.context: Prospect worries about hidden professional services and premium connector costs surfacing after architecture review. — OrbitFlow commits to price services separately and to mark unknowns as to-be-determined.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine.
evidence.context: Usage overages could make the second-year invoice unpredictable, and finance would dislike it even if the base price is fine. — Prior vendor experience; vendor declined to promise a cap before modelling volumes and proposed contractual overage terms.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: If I emit a business event and it triggers a workflow that fans out to five subflows, is that one run or six?
evidence.context: Prospect is concerned that a subflow fan-out might be billed as multiple runs, which would make the recommended composition pattern expensive. — Pricing concern; OrbitFlow rep could not confirm billing semantics from memory and promised a written answer.

claims.text: Security and compliance gates: BrightPath said the BAA is a hard gate and that price is irrelevant until it is resolved. DeltaWorks has a 240-question questionnaire and works council delay risk. Harbor Legal raised ethical walls and UK residency. EU or UK data residency came up at BrightPath, Cedar & Finch, DeltaWorks, Harbor, Greenline and Juniper. Written or contractual no-training assurance was demanded at Acme, BrightPath and Fable.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: The BAA is the gate. If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information.
evidence.context: Prospect (security architect) says the BAA is a hard gate; without one, OrbitFlow cannot be used for any workflow that may involve PHI. — Security gate raised first, stated as non-negotiable. Maya declined to give a yes on the call and committed to a written legal/compliance position within a week; Elliot said a verbal 'working on it' is not acceptable.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: Procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security tells us whether the BAA requirement can be met. If the answer's no, the price is irrelevant.
evidence.context: Prospect will not engage on pricing until the BAA/security question is resolved; price is irrelevant if the answer is no. — Priya explicitly said this was not a negotiating position. Vendor quoted Growth from $1,800/month and said Enterprise is the relevant tier.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: It is two hundred and forty questions.
evidence.context: Prospect's governance team requires a long list of security and compliance items (SAML, SCIM, audit logs, IP restrictions, private connectivity, DR docs, pen tests, EU data residency) and a 240-question questionnaire before proceeding. — Anika frames it as a normal list, not difficulty; OrbitFlow commits to complete the questionnaire and answer 'no' rather than 'partially'.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: Six is realistic if the use case is contested.
evidence.context: Prospect's works council (Betriebsrat) co-determination could delay the project by about six months if workflows monitor employee activity. — Anika raises it as a non-technology gate; Jon asks a clarifying question and offers designing team-level aggregation to address it.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: We do not have a native concept of a matter-level ethical wall that reads your barrier definitions from iManage and enforces them dynamically. That does not exist.
evidence.context: Matter-level information barriers (ethical walls) are a major concern. OrbitFlow staff admitted there is no native matter-level ethical wall that reads barrier definitions from iManage and enforces them dynamically. — Customer called it 'the big one'. Nina said plainly this does not exist out of the box and that the workaround is customer-maintained design. Samir said barriers change weekly, so the maintenance burden is a real cost. Phase one was scoped to barrier-free matters as a result.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: For some of our clients that distinction matters a great deal.
evidence.context: UK data residency is a potential deal gate. OrbitFlow only offers EU residency on Enterprise, and UK residency is unconfirmed. — Customer said some clients, especially public sector, need UK specifically. Nina would not say yes on the call and promised a written answer. Samir insisted a no must be stated as a no, not a roadmap item.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: We're a US operation with a UK subsidiary. What's the default region?
evidence.context: Prospect raised US/UK data residency as an open concern, since they are a US company with a UK subsidiary. — Vendor said default region depends on provisioning and would confirm in writing rather than guess.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. On Growth, I'd need to confirm the default processing region for you in writing rather than guess.
evidence.context: EU data residency is only on Enterprise tier; default processing region on Growth is unconfirmed, and Enterprise is the expensive tier. — Security/data-location concern tied to UK/EU customers; vendor deferred on Growth.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: It depends on which entity the data belongs to, and that is a question for our legal team, not for you.
evidence.context: Prospect's EU/German data residency requirement may not be met by OrbitFlow's EU-only offering; it depends on legal entity classification. — OrbitFlow states it has EU residency but no German region; prospect says EU may be sufficient pending legal review.

evidence.speaker: Lucy Hart
evidence.quote: It's more that our procurement people prefer it.
evidence.context: Preference (not requirement) for UK data residency, which is unconfirmed for OrbitFlow; procurement prefers it — Jon said EU residency is available on Enterprise but UK must be confirmed; Lucy clarified it is not a regulatory mandate

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: We have EU customers and a data residency commitment in some contracts. So EU residency is probably the requirement.
evidence.context: Prospect has EU data residency commitments in enterprise contracts, which is a gating requirement; the sponsor was unsure how many contracts exist. — Security/compliance requirement; OrbitFlow said EU residency is Enterprise-only and advised checking before evaluation.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: That last one needs to be in writing. Not in a demo.
evidence.context: Prospect requires that no-training on customer workflow content be documented in writing, not just stated in a demo. — Condition for trust; vendor agreed it belongs in the contract.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: That last sentence. Is it in the contract or is it on a marketing page?
evidence.context: Prospect wants a no-training commitment to be contractual, not just marketing-page language. — Vendor said it 'needs to be in the contract for you to rely on it'; Elliot said he will insist on that.

evidence.speaker: Ben Foster
evidence.quote: Can we see that in writing?
evidence.context: Prospect requires written assurance that client documents are not used to train models, due to client sensitivity. — Security/data concern; vendor said it is in terms and would send DPA.

claims.text: Several prospects wanted generative AI excluded or deferred from phase one (BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Harbor Legal, Acme). Ember said an AI model in a decision path triggers a nine-month model-risk process. Others doubted AI accuracy (Fable, Inkwell) or distrusted agents (Acme).

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: The second one. That separation would help a lot, actually. AI is interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation use case over.
evidence.context: Prospect's concern about LLM/AI data handling was significant enough to want AI excluded from phase one; they accepted deferring AI review to a separate track. — Elliot called it 'the one I actually care about'. Vendor offered disabling AI or scoping phase one to deterministic steps. Priya noted it was a bigger concession than usual.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: I do not want that review sitting on the critical path of a project whose value comes from something else entirely.
evidence.context: Prospect does not want generative AI in phase one because it would add data protection, works council and legal review to the critical path. — OrbitFlow says AI steps are optional and can be disabled on Enterprise; Anika wants contractual assurance that customer content is not used for training.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: I'm much more sceptical about generative AI than Eleanor is.
evidence.context: Generative AI is a reservation. Samir wants AI features disabled entirely for phase one, and Eleanor says the firm's second use case is AI-based. — Samir is more sceptical of generative AI than Eleanor. Nina confirmed AI can be disabled on Enterprise. Eleanor treats it as phase-one only and wants it kept on the table.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: AI's interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation case over.
evidence.context: Security review is not a blocker; AI usage and LLM data handling may need separate review and could be scoped out. — Customer said separation would help and AI is not worth blocking automation; vendor offered to disable AI or scope pilot to deterministic steps.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: getting something into scope is a nine-month process here.
evidence.context: Putting an AI model into a decision path would bring it under the prospect's model risk management framework, which takes about nine months. — Hannah explained the internal model-risk policy. Nina Patel responded that AI steps are explicit, optional, and can be disabled by admins, but did not fully resolve the scope concern.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: If it tells me four accounts are overdue and actually it's six, that's worse than nothing.
evidence.context: Prospect doubts the AI weekly summary can be trusted for accuracy; inaccurate overdue counts would be worse than nothing. — Concern about AI accuracy; vendor deflected to 'very good' models and checking underlying data.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: If there isn't a theme this week, will it invent one?
evidence.context: Concern that the AI weekly summary could invent themes when none exist. — Jon Bell said the workflow should refuse thin cases via minimum-evidence rules rather than relying on model confidence.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I'm wary of the word agent, mostly because it usually means nobody can explain why something happened.
evidence.context: Prospect is wary of AI agents because they can obscure why something happened. — Reservation about agent-style AI; vendor framed AI as optional, inspectable steps.

claims.text: Status quo or existing tools were named as the real alternative: Workato at Acme, Power Automate at BrightPath and Greenline, Zapier at Cedar & Finch and Fable, keeping scripts at Ember, Gainsight at Inkwell, and in-house builds at Harbor Legal and Juniper (Step Functions or Retool).

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: And the honest comparison is Workato, or just improving what we already have. Not doing nothing.
evidence.context: Status quo (Workato or improving existing process) is the honest comparison, and 'do nothing' is not the alternative. — Customer and vendor agreed the pilot should be defined against status quo and alternatives; vendor said 'don't buy OrbitFlow' is a valid outcome.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: Power Automate. Or just improving what we already have.
evidence.context: Status quo and Microsoft Power Automate are the real competitors; Power Automate is already covered by their Microsoft agreement, which matters to procurement. — Vendor said a 'don't buy' outcome is valid if the existing approach meets criteria more cheaply. Earlier Priya said Power Automate is already covered by the Microsoft agreement.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us. Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it. For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
evidence.context: Biggest concern: OrbitFlow lacks a first-class Dynamics connector, and Power Automate is already embedded, so OrbitFlow must be materially better to justify a switch — Stated after Jon Bell candidly said OrbitFlow does not have the deepest first-class Dynamics connector; Carlos framed the gap as the core obstacle given the incumbent

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership.
evidence.context: Budget is the biggest risk; prospect may conclude they are over-buying and keep Zapier with better documentation and ownership. — Sophie framed a no-buy outcome as legitimate; Leo said he'd rather learn that in July than month five.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough for a company that doesn't have an IT team.
evidence.context: Prospect may choose Zapier plus better process discipline instead, given price and complexity risks and no IT team. — Competing-tool alternative raised as a real possibility; prospect said she would be doing her job badly not to consider it.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
evidence.context: The main alternative is keeping existing scripts and documenting them better, which is cheaper and likely to be proposed internally, and could delay the project by about two months. — Hannah said it would not satisfy the auditor but could still win internal support; vendor responded by addressing it in the pilot criteria.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: It's the alternative I'd propose if the cost comparison favoured it.
evidence.context: Expanding the existing Gainsight deployment is the competing alternative the prospect would consider if cost favours it. — Competitive objection. Maya Chen said the comparison should be done honestly rather than ignoring the competition.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: the counter-argument is that they then own it forever and they're already at capacity.
evidence.context: Internal development is a competing alternative. Eleanor says the internal team is already at capacity and the build option would mean owning the solution indefinitely. — Samir said some people favour building in-house. Eleanor said the argument for it is that the firm understands its own systems better than a vendor.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: I think most of what you do could be built internally. We have the skills. The question is whether we should.
evidence.context: Prospect's core reservation is that building internally with Step Functions or Retool Workflows is a credible alternative, and that maintenance ownership is the real cost. — Build-vs-buy objection; the sponsor (Marcus) argued maintenance is the real cost and the person who would own it is overloaded.

claims.text: Internal approval and timing hurdles: Cedar & Finch can only approve under $15k/year and the $21.6k cost goes to the COO and finance director. Fable needs founder approval above £20k. Greenline's Microsoft platform team will likely oppose, and no decision is expected this year. BrightPath has no production launch before Q4. DeltaWorks has six stakeholders who can block. Inkwell's finance has effective veto.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
evidence.context: Budget approval threshold: prospect can only approve tools under $15k/year; the $21.6k annual cost goes to COO and finance director, a slower process. — Internal approval hesitation; the buyer's stated reason for delay.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
evidence.context: Spend above £20k needs founder approval, which is a hard internal limit; prospect needs a stronger value justification than 'more robust' versus Zapier at about £2k. — Internal approval barrier; prospect said the conversation upstairs will focus on ROI versus Zapier.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The Microsoft platform team will not want this. Not because it's bad. Because it isn't Microsoft.
evidence.context: Internal approval risk: the Microsoft platform team will strongly oppose OrbitFlow because it is not Microsoft, and they have killed things before — Carlos says formal role is influence, practically depends on how strongly they object; Lucy adds they have a track record of killing tools

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Realistically, no. I want to be straight with you about that rather than let you forecast something that isn't there.
evidence.context: Timing: no decision this year; any purchase would have to fit the October budgeting cycle for next fiscal year — Carlos described the process as early exploration, explicitly not procurement, and was candid that a decision is unlikely this year

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: No production launch before Q4. That's firm.
evidence.context: Timing constraint: no production launch before Q4; only a non-sensitive proof of concept is possible sooner. A successful pilot would not automatically mean broad deployment. — Priya said pilot and broad deployment are two decisions with different approvers. Vendor said it would rather hear this now.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Regional IT cannot say no formally but can make implementation impossible, which amounts to the same thing.
evidence.context: Prospect's decision involves six stakeholders, and architecture board and information security can unilaterally block; regional IT can make implementation impossible. — Martin describes the approval order; procurement is last and slow.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: Finance can say not yet, which is the same thing in practice.
evidence.context: Finance and security have effective veto power; Darren would block if the data does not support the project. — Internal approval hurdles. Olivia said Finance saying not yet is equivalent to no in practice.

claims.text: Integration and architecture fit worried several prospects: DeltaWorks (on-premise and SAP reachability, German plants), Ember (event bus not reachable, schema changes), Greenline (no first-class Dynamics connector, offline connectivity), Cedar & Finch (Shopify trigger must be native) and Juniper (Salesforce API limits). Harbor Legal said integration effort could be disproportionate.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Because if the deployment architecture doesn't work, the product is irrelevant. We have bought software before that demonstrated beautifully and then could not reach our systems.
evidence.context: Prospect hesitates on deployment architecture: systems that cannot be exposed to the public internet cannot be reached by a platform calling over the internet. — Martin frames this as a gating concern; Jon responds that an agent or controlled gateway pattern may work but must be validated against the actual environment.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: the biggest issue is whether SAP and our on-premise systems make the implementation too heavy for the first use case. Everything else is manageable.
evidence.context: Prospect states the biggest issue is whether SAP and on-premise systems make implementation too heavy for the first use case; this is the crux of the decision. — Martin says everything else is manageable; if integration needs nine months of work, he would choose a different first use case or not proceed.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: In practice, two German plants are still prohibited from exposing production databases directly to SaaS vendors.
evidence.context: Prospect's two German plants are prohibited from exposing production databases to SaaS vendors, which constrains the architecture; the policy has not been reviewed in eighteen months. — Martin corrects his earlier 'cloud-first' claim; OrbitFlow proposes deferring those plants to phase two.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Not currently.
evidence.context: The internal event bus is not reachable from outside the network, which is a technical blocker for the required integration. — Required integration; vendor said it is a real architecture question and needs a design session.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: We've had integrations fail because someone renamed a field and nothing surfaced.
evidence.context: Schema changes in source systems have caused past integration failures that went unnoticed, which is a concern for the new integration. — Raised as a prior failure pattern; vendor said mapping errors surface on the run and recommended validation; Hannah wants bad-data testing.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us. Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it. For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
evidence.context: Biggest concern: OrbitFlow lacks a first-class Dynamics connector, and Power Automate is already embedded, so OrbitFlow must be materially better to justify a switch — Stated after Jon Bell candidly said OrbitFlow does not have the deepest first-class Dynamics connector; Carlos framed the gap as the core obstacle given the incumbent

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: this is the thing that kills most vendors.
evidence.context: Offline and intermittent connectivity is a hard constraint that many vendors fail on; he expects demos that assume real-time connectivity to fail — Raised by the customer as a make-or-break requirement from field sites with poor signal; Jon responded with sync-event and timeout patterns and offered a live demo

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
evidence.context: Shopify trigger must be native and event-driven; a polling workaround is a dealbreaker. Vendor could not confirm trigger coverage and deferred to a written answer. — Integration concern; vendor did not confirm.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: Salesforce API limits are the constraint. We've hit them before.
evidence.context: Prospect names the Salesforce API limits as a hard constraint that could block the design; they have hit them before. — Integration/rate-limit concern; OrbitFlow proposed batching or caching if the allocation is insufficient.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: My concern — and I'd say it's the biggest risk to this whole thing — is that our security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate.
evidence.context: Samir Khan says security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate to the value, calling it the biggest risk to the whole project. — Customer's main reservation, raised at the steering-meeting level. Leo responded that he would test it with an operation-by-operation difficulty assessment and a services estimate rather than argue it.

claims.text: Maintenance, ownership and adoption risk: Acme feared a tool the team must babysit, and its operators must believe they can own it. BrightPath feared users would route around workflows. Inkwell raised key-person dependency, and Juniper's sponsor feared only the engineer would understand the workflows.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: I want to make sure we don't buy a tool that looks great in a demo and then becomes another thing my team has to babysit.
evidence.context: Concern that a demo looks great but becomes another thing the team must babysit; wary of hidden scaling and fragility. — Customer's concern about tools that become maintenance burdens and depend on individuals; vendor pointed to run history and ownership features.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: And the people who'll operate it have to believe they can own it — that last one is not a small thing.
evidence.context: Prospect expects the decision to slip and wants the operating team to believe they can own the workflow. — Timing concern: choose vendor by end of July, first workflows live in September; customer says it will slip. Ownership by operators is a key decision condition.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation.
evidence.context: Prospect worries that adoption will fail, with users routing around a technically correct workflow, as happened with a previous internal tool. — Raised in the pilot-measurement discussion; Priya wants adoption measured alongside technical success.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: I want to know that if I get hit by a bus, someone else can pick this up.
evidence.context: Key-person dependency risk: the project could be lost if its owner leaves, as happened with Gainsight. — Jon Bell said this is mostly an operating-model issue, not a product answer.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: I've also seen teams buy a platform to avoid maintenance and then spend a year maintaining the integration to the platform.
evidence.context: Prospect worries that teams buy a platform to avoid maintenance and then spend a year maintaining the integration to it. — Maintenance-cost concern; OrbitFlow agreed it happens and proposed testing time consumed over four weeks.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: If we end up with something only Ava understands, we've spent money to move the problem.
evidence.context: Prospect's sponsor is worried the workflows will be understandable only by the engineer, which would move the problem rather than solve it. — Comprehensibility and adoption concern; OrbitFlow admitted complex canvases are unreadable by default and that there is no linter enforcing composition.

not_covered: No frequency count per reason was computed; ranking reflects how many calls raised each theme, based on the findings listed.
assumptions: 'Prospects' interpreted as Prospect call type (new business) only, excluding Renewal, Churn post-mortem, and Cold call calls.
'Most common' requires aggregating reasons across calls, so each call is read for its underlying stated objections rather than for a frequency count.
Only Prospect call type (new business) is included, per the stated assumption.
Theme ordering is read from the findings, not from code-computed counts.

grades.reason: Section [3] covers reliable integrations with system of record, with specific connectors named (Salesforce, SAP, Dynamics, Shopify, Postgres).
Section [1] covers SSO/SCIM, exportable audit logs to own systems (BrightPath, DeltaWorks), and audit controls. Least-privilege is only in a Juniper quote, but the core is covered.

Section [2] covers run history/failure visibility and alerts; Ember's retry semantics quote and exception queues appear. Acme's metrics in their own monitoring isn't explicit, but reliability/observability is covered.
The answer covers no-training AI terms (Acme, BrightPath, Ember) in [1], but not Ember's per-workspace AI disablement or BrightPath's LLM data handling as AI controls specifically.

answer.question: What product capabilities appear to be most important to prospects?
answer.answer: Across all 10 prospect calls, the most consistent priorities were security and audit controls (SSO/SCIM, exportable audit logs, no-training AI terms, data residency) [1], run history and failure visibility [2], and reliable integrations with the prospect's system of record [3]. Team-owned exception queues, change control and reusable components also recurred [4][5], while some priorities were call-specific [6].

claims.text: Security and compliance requirements were raised by most prospects. SSO/SCIM was raised by Acme, BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember and Juniper, with Cedar & Finch calling SSO nice-to-have and Fable Media wanting Google login or SAML. Prospects named exportable audit logs into their own systems (BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember, Harbor Legal) and contractual or written no-training AI terms (Acme, BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember, Fable Media, Inkwell). EU or UK data residency came up at BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember, Harbor Legal and Juniper. BrightPath called the BAA the gate, and Ember named model-risk and auditability as gates. The vendor said SAML SSO/SCIM and audit export are Enterprise-only.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise.
evidence.context: Security baseline required: SOC 2 Type II, SSO, audit logs; SAML SSO and SCIM are Enterprise-only per vendor. — Security is not a gate per Rachel; SSO is a standard requirement.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: The BAA is the gate. If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information.
evidence.context: Security/compliance review is the gate: a BAA is required before OrbitFlow can be used for any workflow that may involve PHI; without it, nothing else proceeds. — Prospect's stated deal-breaker; vendor declined to give a yes on the call and promised a written position in a week.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: we need to resolve the BAA question, review your subprocessors, SSO and SCIM, understand retention, and confirm how US data is handled.
evidence.context: Prospect's security list included SSO and SCIM provisioning, subprocessor review, retention controls, and US data handling; vendor said SAML SSO and SCIM are on Enterprise. — Security checklist raised before any demo; vendor confirmed baseline capabilities.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, both on Enterprise.
evidence.context: Vendor stated SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are available only on the Enterprise package. — Vendor capability claim on baseline certifications.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: If it only lives in your console it's not an audit trail, it's a screenshot.
evidence.context: Prospect requires audit logs to be exportable to their own SIEM; an audit trail living only in the vendor console is not acceptable. — Audit/compliance requirement raised during security discussion.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: SSO would be nice rather than mandatory
evidence.context: Prospect wants SSO as a nice-to-have rather than mandatory, plus a standard DPA and clarity on UK/EU data processing location (EU residency stated as Enterprise-only). — Security requirements raised during demo; vendor confirmed EU residency only on Enterprise.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: SAML, SCIM, audit logs, IP restrictions, role separation, private connectivity options, disaster recovery documentation, penetration test material, and German or EU data residency.
evidence.context: Customer requires SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning as governance items; vendor says both are supported on Enterprise. — Headline governance requirement from the customer's IT governance lead; vendor stated support in response.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning — both supported, both on Enterprise.
evidence.context: Vendor states SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported and available on the Enterprise package. — Vendor capability claim made in response to the governance list.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: can audit data be exported to our own systems? We do not accept a vendor console as an audit trail.
evidence.context: Customer requires audit logs that can be exported to its own systems; it does not accept a vendor console as the audit trail. — Governance requirement; vendor said audit export is available on Enterprise.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: That last point needs to be contractual.
evidence.context: Customer requires AI features to be disableable and contractually guaranteed not to train on customer workflow content; vendor says Enterprise can disable AI and does not train shared models on customer content. — Customer excludes generative AI from phase one; vendor states controls.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: The main gates are model-risk and auditability. If you can't satisfy those, connector breadth will not save the project.
evidence.context: Prospect states model-risk and auditability are the gating requirements; connector breadth will not save the project if these are not satisfied. — Hannah Cole, Senior Risk Engineer, on what could kill the deal; she treats these as deal-breakers.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: The list is: SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, exportable audit history, retention controls, encryption details, subprocessor review, EU residency for European records, and contractual language that our data is not used to train shared AI models.
evidence.context: Prospect's audit requirement list includes SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, exportable audit history, retention controls, encryption, subprocessor review, EU residency, and contractual no-training language. — Security/compliance checklist Hannah requires before she will approve.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise.
evidence.context: Vendor states SAML SSO and SCIM are available only on the Enterprise package, and audit export is Enterprise-only. — Vendor answer to the security checklist; relevant to SSO as a requirement.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: On exportable audit history — define exportable. Because I've had vendors mean "you can download a CSV from a UI" and that is not exportable.
evidence.context: Prospect requires exportable, programmatic audit history (API/webhook into their SIEM), not a UI CSV download; this is a key differentiator against Tray. — Hannah pressed for a definition of 'exportable' and said programmatic export is what would decide the choice.

evidence.speaker: Ben Foster
evidence.quote: We'd want Google login or SAML, normal GDPR terms
evidence.context: Prospect requires SSO via Google login or SAML; vendor said SSO is included on all plans, but the prospect doubts it and asked for confirmation. — Security requirement; prospect says competitors gate SSO to enterprise tiers. Vendor said 'fairly sure' and would confirm.

evidence.speaker: Ben Foster
evidence.quote: written reassurance that our client documents aren't used to train models. Some of our clients are quite sensitive about that.
evidence.context: Prospect requires written assurance that client documents are not used to train AI models, due to client sensitivity. — Data-privacy requirement; vendor promised a DPA.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: Your console is not an audit trail as far as I'm concerned.
evidence.context: Prospect requires SIEM-grade audit export; the console alone is not considered an audit trail. Vendor said audit export is on Enterprise and events can be forwarded via APIs/webhooks. — Security/compliance requirement for audit logs.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. UK specifically I need to confirm in writing.
evidence.context: Prospect has a hard compliance requirement for UK data residency; vendor offers only EU residency (Enterprise) and could not confirm UK, so it may be a gate. — Public sector clients make the EU/UK distinction material; vendor to confirm in writing within a week.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: That last one matters for us.
evidence.context: Olivia says it matters to Inkwell that the vendor does not use customer workflow content to train a shared model. — Responds to the vendor's statement that customer workflow content is not used for training. Relevant to AI-feature requirements.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: SSO and SCIM. Secrets management, which we've covered. Audit logs. Least-privilege credentials. Regional controls.
evidence.context: Prospect requires security controls: SSO and SCIM, secrets management, audit logs, least-privilege credentials, and EU data residency (required by two enterprise contracts). Vendor stated SAML SSO and SCIM are Enterprise-only and EU residency is Enterprise-only. — Security list gating the deal; EU residency sourced from prospect contracts.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise.
evidence.context: Customer requires EU data residency for data; the vendor says EU residency is available on Enterprise but no German region exists. — Data residency requirement; customer says EU may suffice pending legal review.

claims.text: Run history, debugging and failure visibility were repeatedly emphasised. Acme, BrightPath and DeltaWorks each said they can see that something was late but not why or which dependency failed. Cedar & Finch learns of failures only when customers complain and wants failure-rate alerts. Ember named debugging and a programmatic audit trail as the deciders against Tray. Greenline wants supervisors to understand failures without raising tickets, and Juniper wants run events via API.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same thing happened fifteen times last month.
evidence.context: Operational telemetry and visibility into why a process failed is a key gap; prospect wants to know which dependency failed and how often issues recur. — Pain is about root cause and recurrence, not just outcome lateness.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same failure happened fifteen times last month.
evidence.context: Prospect's core operational requirement is observable run history and telemetry: they can see outcomes but cannot diagnose why workflows were late or which dependency failed. — Current-state pain; prospect values run history over connector count.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: We can tell you something was late. We are much worse at telling you why, or which dependency failed
evidence.context: Vendor states the platform records and visualises run history, letting admins see inputs, steps and failure points; the customer lacks operational telemetry on why processes stall. — Customer pain point on observability that the platform addresses.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Lee
evidence.quote: When a customer complains.
evidence.context: Prospect's core pain is detection of broken automations; failures are currently discovered only when customers complain, and run history visibility is sought. — Marcus describes the current detection mechanism; vendor demoed run history.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Can I set an alert on a failure rate rather than an individual failure? Because sixty automations, if I get an email per failure I'll just filter them into a folder and never look at it.
evidence.context: Prospect values monitoring/alerting on failure rates rather than per-failure notifications, to avoid alert fatigue across ~60 automations. — Customer-stated priority on monitoring; Sophie explains why per-failure alerts would be ignored.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
evidence.context: Prospect says the deciding factors versus Tray are debugging experience and a genuinely programmatic audit export. — Asked what must be true to choose OrbitFlow over Tray.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: It's the debugging loop and it's error handling. Retry semantics were opaque. We couldn't always tell whether something had run twice.
evidence.context: Prospect's top operational pain is weak debugging and retry visibility in large visual workflows; idempotency/retry semantics were opaque in the Tray PoC. — Feedback from the Tray proof of concept.

evidence.speaker: Lucy Hart
evidence.quote: If a regional supervisor can look at a failed thing and understand what happened without raising a ticket to Carlos's team, that's material.
evidence.context: Troubleshooting ease is a key differentiator the prospect needs: supervisors should understand failures without raising tickets to central ops, since complex Power Automate flows are hard to debug. — Pain with incumbent Power Automate; operations team of six supports 2,500 people.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: Okay. That's a limitation but it's not a blocker.
evidence.context: Prospect requires a run-record and observability capability: run events available via API for forwarding into their own observability, and manual re-trigger; prospect treats lack of deterministic replay as a limitation, not a blocker. — Vendor demo of run record; replay gap acknowledged.

claims.text: Reliable integrations were a priority, with prospects ranking by system of record rather than connector count. Acme and BrightPath said an unreliable system-of-record connector (Salesforce at Acme) is the deal-breaker. Ember said connector breadth is a tie. Juniper deprioritises logo count in favour of webhooks, REST and a safe Postgres connector. Specific gaps: Greenline's first-class Dynamics connector is its biggest issue; DeltaWorks's SAP/on-premise connectivity is decisive and the vendor offered no one-click SAP connector; Harbor Legal's iManage/Intapp need API-only integration; Cedar & Finch needs a native Shopify trigger, which the vendor could not confirm. Several prospects also want schema-change detection after silent integration failures (Acme, BrightPath, Ember).

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: The system of record. If that connector's unreliable, none of the rest matters. After that it's the collaboration and data systems
evidence.context: Salesforce connector reliability is the deal-breaker; collaboration and data systems (Slack, Snowflake) next. — Prospect ranks integrations by importance.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: The system of record. If that connector's unreliable none of the rest matters.
evidence.context: Prospect's must-have integrations are HubSpot, Teams, Jira and Azure AD, with the system-of-record connector as the deal-breaker; Databricks is not phase one. — Integration priorities; vendor said connectors must be validated per operation, not by logo.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
evidence.context: Prospect says the deciding factors versus Tray are debugging experience and a genuinely programmatic audit export. — Asked what must be true to choose OrbitFlow over Tray.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: I don't care how many logos are on your integrations page. I care about webhooks, REST, and whether the Postgres connector does anything stupid.
evidence.context: Prospect values developer-quality APIs (webhooks, REST) and version control over a large connector catalogue. — Vendor recap of prior email; prospect explicitly deprioritises catalogue size.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: Holds connections open. Doesn't respect statement timeouts. Runs unbounded queries against production.
evidence.context: Prospect requires Postgres connector that does not hold connections open, respects statement timeouts, and avoids unbounded queries against production. — Explicit deal-breaker-style technical concern about the Postgres connector.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us.
evidence.context: The prospect's most important requirement is a first-class Dynamics integration; the vendor's lack of a deepest first-class Dynamics connector is the biggest issue for them, since Power Automate is already embedded. — Customer states this as the decisive issue; vendor admits the gap. Dynamics 365 and Teams are mandatory.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: the biggest issue is whether SAP and our on-premise systems make the implementation too heavy for the first use case. Everything else is manageable.
evidence.context: Customer names SAP S/4HANA connectivity and on-premise SQL Server connectivity as the decisive capability for the first use case; the vendor has not yet shown a viable SAP route. — Customer states this is the crux of whether the deal proceeds; vendor offered API, REST, and agent/gateway options without a one-click SAP connector.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: What I will not do is tell you there's a one-click SAP connector that solves your estate
evidence.context: Vendor declines to claim a one-click SAP connector; offers API-based options, generic REST action, and agent/gateway pattern for on-premise. — Vendor capability statement on SAP integration, explicitly hedged.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: our security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate.
evidence.context: Prospect's main concern is integration effort into iManage and Intapp, which lack native connectors; vendor confirmed only API-based integration via generic REST and webhooks, requiring maintenance. — Key integration requirement and the decisive question for the deal; prospect worries effort is disproportionate to value.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: A native Shopify trigger is — that's important. If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
evidence.context: Native, event-driven Shopify trigger is a must-have; a polling-based integration would not interest the prospect. Vendor could not confirm trigger coverage and deferred to a written answer. — Shopify is the most critical integration; vendor was unsure and promised written follow-up.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: We've had integrations die because someone renamed a field or added a picklist value, and the automation just — didn't say anything.
evidence.context: Schema-change and mapping-error detection is a requirement; silent integration failures are a past problem. — Prior integrations broke silently after field renames.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: A demo with clean data proves nothing.
evidence.context: Prospect requires schema-change handling and validation: they have had integrations break silently from renamed fields and want this tested with messy data. — Reliability concern; prospect wants it in the evaluation.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: We've had integrations fail because someone renamed a field and nothing surfaced.
evidence.context: Prospect requires schema-change detection and bad-data testing for integrations after a field rename went unnoticed. — Past integration failure drives the requirement.

claims.text: Prospects wanted exception and queue ownership assigned to teams rather than named individuals, because role churn breaks current automations. This was raised at Acme, BrightPath, Cedar & Finch, DeltaWorks, Ember and Inkwell (escalation routing to a group).

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: Can the queue be owned by a team? Not a named person. People change roles constantly here and individual ownership is genuinely one of the reasons our current stuff breaks.
evidence.context: Queue/exception ownership must be assignable to a team, not a named person, because individual ownership causes current breakage. — Tom ties this to role churn and current failures.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: individual ownership is one of the main reasons our current automations rot.
evidence.context: Prospect requires exception and queue ownership by teams rather than named individuals, since individual ownership causes automations to rot. — Ownership requirement tied to role churn in current Power Automate flows.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Owned by who?
evidence.context: Prospect requires an error-proof exception path when order data is incomplete, with ownership by a team rather than an individual. — Sophie probed handling of incomplete order data during the workflow demo.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: Can the exception queue be owned by a team rather than a named individual?
evidence.context: Customer requires exception queues owned by teams rather than individuals, and field-level masking of payloads; vendor said masking is a design conversation, not a checkbox. — Governance and visibility requirement; customer notes individual ownership causes automations to decay.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Build it, change it, break it, roll it back. Not just build it.
evidence.context: Prospect requires a change-management evaluation (dev/prod separation, versioning, rollback) and team-owned exception queues with on-call fallback. — Environment and ownership requirements raised late in the call.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: That happens constantly.
evidence.context: Olivia reports that routing escalations to a named CSM breaks constantly because of role changes, so routing to a group is needed. — Vendor proposed routing to a group or dynamic field; the customer confirmed the problem is frequent.

claims.text: Change control and reuse were recurring needs. Version history and change visibility were sought at Acme, BrightPath, Ember and Inkwell (diffable logic), and DeltaWorks called separate dev/test/prod environments non-negotiable. Reusable templates or subflows were valued at BrightPath, Cedar & Finch (called most compelling), Greenline and Harbor Legal.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: if someone changes a condition on a Friday afternoon and it breaks, can we see exactly what changed?
evidence.context: Version history and change control of workflows is a requirement. — Concern about Friday changes breaking flows.

evidence.speaker: Jon Bell
evidence.quote: Version history and change metadata, yes. Rollback and promotion patterns vary by workflow and package.
evidence.context: Prospect wants version history and change metadata to see what changed when a workflow breaks; vendor offered version history and change metadata, with rollback varying by package. — Change-management requirement.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Build it, change it, break it, roll it back. Not just build it.
evidence.context: Prospect requires a change-management evaluation (dev/prod separation, versioning, rollback) and team-owned exception queues with on-call fallback. — Environment and ownership requirements raised late in the call.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: I'm not having business-critical logic that only exists in a web UI.
evidence.context: Darren requires workflow logic to be version-controlled or at least reviewable, and asks whether two versions can be diffed. — Vendor said there is version history and API export but no git integration; a true side-by-side diff was not confirmed.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: That is not negotiable. We do not put anything into production that has not been through test
evidence.context: Customer requires separate dev, test and production workspaces with change control, and a second approver; vendor says workspace separation is supported with version history, with rollback/promotion gaps to be mapped. — Deal-level non-negotiable on environment separation.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: That's — okay, that's actually the interesting bit for me. That's the backlog answer, potentially.
evidence.context: Prospect wants reusable components so the systems group can build subflows the business assembles, reducing the backlog. — Prospect sees this as the backlog answer; ties to a stated 11-week backlog.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: That is the most compelling thing you've said.
evidence.context: Prospect views reusable templates/subflows as the capability that best addresses their maintenance problem across many automations. — Sophie says the templates speak to the actual problem; vendor pitched consolidating ~60 Zaps into fewer subflows.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: if we build the remediation pattern once and use it in eight regions, rather than eight regions each building their own.
evidence.context: Reusability of remediation patterns across regions is a key requirement the prospect wants proven (build once, use in eight regions). — Vendor agreed to test it rather than claim it.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: Monitoring, mostly. And reusable components.
evidence.context: Prospect wants improved monitoring and reusable components beyond their current Power Automate tool, which is used for low-risk admin tasks. — Reason for evaluating OrbitFlow over incumbent.

claims.text: Some priorities were specific to one prospect. Greenline needs offline and no-signal tolerance. Harbor Legal needs a write-proof conflicts system and matter-level ethical walls, which the vendor said do not exist natively. Fable Media wants a no-code, flexible builder and rejected governance and audit as irrelevant to an agency. Inkwell wants escalation and trustworthy AI summaries. Juniper's per-event and subflow billing concerns are cost-driven.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Correct. And this is the thing that kills most vendors.
evidence.context: Offline tolerance is a hard design constraint: field connectivity is intermittent, so workflows cannot assume the mobile app is online, and the prospect wants the 'not hearing' case handled as an event. — Raised by vendor from notes; customer confirmed and described poor coverage at Scottish and Welsh sites.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: Conflicts is not negotiable. If a workflow makes a conflicts decision, we're finished.
evidence.context: Prospect treats conflicts decisions as untouchable; workflow must not have any write path to the conflicts system, enforced at the credential/permission level, not just by design intent. — Security constraint stated as a deal-breaker-level requirement by the prospect's information security manager; vendor responded with read-only connection scoping as the control.

evidence.speaker: Nina Patel
evidence.quote: We do not have a native concept of a matter-level ethical wall that reads your barrier definitions from iManage and enforces them dynamically. That does not exist.
evidence.context: Prospect requires matter-level ethical information barriers enforced by the system. Vendor stated OrbitFlow does NOT have a native matter-level ethical wall that reads barrier definitions from iManage; this is a real unsolved gap that must be designed around and maintained. — Vendor limitation admitted; barriers change weekly, creating an ongoing maintenance burden. Phase one scoped to barrier-free matters.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: We don't have a dedicated IT team. At all. An operations manager would administer this.
evidence.context: Prospect has no IT team; the product must be no-code enough for an operations manager to administer. — Usability requirement; vendor said it is completely no-code.

evidence.speaker: Ben Foster
evidence.quote: So if the pitch is "we'll standardise your onboarding", that's going to meet resistance from me.
evidence.context: Prospect's onboarding customisation per client-services pod must be supported; they reject a rigid standardised workflow. — Requirement for flexible configuration; vendor claimed full flexibility and that pod customisation is configuration.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: We're an agency, Alastair. Nobody's auditing our onboarding process.
evidence.context: Prospect's must-have is a capability to compare-check accuracy and reliability of automation; prospect is not interested in governance/audit features, seeing them as irrelevant to an agency. — Vendor pitched governance and audit trail as differentiators; prospect rejected the relevance.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: The escalation. That's the bit I want.
evidence.context: Olivia names the escalation path as the key capability she wants from the workflow. — Prospect's stated priority: an alert without escalation is a notification that gets ignored; the customer's Slack alert channel is already full.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: Because otherwise it's just a plausible paragraph.
evidence.context: Olivia wants the weekly AI summary to replace a spreadsheet nobody reads, and it must be trustworthy. — Second requested capability: a weekly narrative summary of customer themes with links back to source tickets and accounts.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: What I do not want is to pay you per event.
evidence.context: Prospect's top volume concern: cannot pay per raw event; only business-relevant events should trigger workflows, and vendor agreed event filtering should stay in the customer's AWS layer. — Millions of product events per day from Segment; cost-driven architecture requirement.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: If it's six, the composition pattern you're recommending is also the expensive pattern, and that's a conflict I'd want surfaced before we commit.
evidence.context: Prospect's key pricing/architecture question: whether subflow invocations count as separate billable runs, which would make the recommended composition pattern expensive. — Vendor could not confirm billing semantics and promised written answer.

conflicts.description: Most prospects treated audit and governance as gating. Fable Media's COO said nobody audits an agency's onboarding and rejected the vendor's governance pitch.
Vendor reps at other calls said SAML SSO/SCIM are Enterprise-only, but on the Fable Media call the vendor said SSO is on all plans (hedged as 'fairly sure'), and the prospect doubted it.
Ember, Juniper and BrightPath de-emphasised connector count in favour of reliability and debugging, while Fable Media needs native connectors for its named stack.

not_covered: Importance was inferred from stated priority and emphasis, not a ranking by the prospects. Deal outcomes were not provided, so it is unknown which capabilities actually decided deals.
assumptions: Question concerns prospect calls only (new business), since prospects are the audience named.

answer.question: What is different about how the sales team handles renewals versus new business?
answer.answer: Renewal calls were run by account staff (CSM Ruth Adeyemi, AE Maya Chen or Leo Grant) in a retention-oriented way: they opened with account facts, cited a standard 7% uplift, right-sized seats, and gave concessions or exit options [1][2][3]. In prospect calls the AEs ran discovery or demos, quoted the $1,800/month Growth list tier and steered larger prospects to custom Enterprise, withheld firm numbers until the user model was known, and set up pilots or evaluations [4][5][6]. Both sides stressed candour, but in renewals it showed up as proactive disclosure and customer-favourable terms [7][8].

answer.question: What did Acme Logistics say about their current workflow?
answer.answer: Acme described a fragmented, weakly owned workflow environment. Their core stack is Salesforce, Slack, Snowflake, Gainsight and Google Sheets, plus an existing Workato contract. The system of record varies by object, and much of the real context lives in chat. Existing automation has no clear owner, escalation depends on who happens to see a stuck item, and people build their own reminders, spreadsheets and scripts (at least three of unknown authorship). Their operational telemetry is weak: they can tell that something was late but not why, or whether it recurred. They also said the process people describe differs from the process people run.

Deployment architecture and governance come first for DeltaWorks, controlled regional building and promotion matters to Greenline, approver-only licensing is a deal-breaker for Greenline, and Juniper wants business teams to change rules without engineering. Handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success run through spreadsheets and Slack reminders, so renewal risks and implementation blockers are noticed late (sometimes a week, sometimes at the QBR). answer.question: Why did customers who left decide to leave?
answer.answer: The two churn post-mortems (CALL-014 Verity Payments and CALL-015 Oakhill Property) show different reasons. Verity moved to Workato: its operations team never built any workflows, so it paid a premium for business-user autonomy and used the platform as an engineering tool. It also had to write custom integrations anyway, Workato's core-banking connector and engineering story were stronger, and engineers wanted to build in-house. Price was only a secondary factor. Oakhill left for Zapier because it bought more than it needed: it was on Growth at $1,800/month with only four active users and simple workflows, and Zapier would cost about a tenth. The product itself worked fine. Both also cited a lack of proactive vendor attention. Separately, Pinewood (CALL-012) is an at-risk renewal, not a confirmed churn, so it is not counted as a departure.

answer.question: Has anyone from the vendor given inconsistent answers about the product?
answer.answer: Yes. The clearest case is Alastair McCrae in CALL-006 (Fable Media), who gave answers that conflict with other OrbitFlow statements, and one claim that turned out wrong in CALL-006 itself. Elsewhere, Jon Bell and Nina Patel gave consistent, hedged answers. Leo Grant and Maya Chen were consistent on pricing and SSO. Alastair's claims: (1) SSO is included on all plans, but other calls say SAML SSO and SCIM are Enterprise-only (and CALL-012 confirms SAML SSO is lost on Growth); he later retreated to 'fairly sure' and said he'd confirm. (2) He said the product is 'completely no-code', while Jon Bell says elsewhere that OrbitFlow does not claim every workflow is no-code. (3) He said date-slip alerting is 'definitely doable', then admitted he'd need to check with an SE whether it takes two workflows. (4) He said monthly billing was 'usually fine' and that the thirty users are 'the package', but then conceded he'd have to check with his manager. (5) He claimed 'up and running in a couple of weeks' and 'September's no problem' with no basis; he also said 'fully GDPR compliant' without support.

answer.question: Which cold calls produced a follow-up, and what did the successful ones have in common?
answer.answer: Four of the five cold calls produced a follow-up: Quarry Ridge Foods (CALL-016), Silverline Travel (CALL-017), Beacon Housing Trust (CALL-018) and Kestrel Robotics (CALL-020). Trafford Dental (CALL-019) did not. Yvonne said she wouldn't read anything sent and concluded "Then we're not it." Quarry Ridge's follow-up is the weakest, a single email in February. What the four had in common: (1) The rep was upfront that it was a cold call, asked permission or let the prospect end it. (2) The rep asked questions and listened rather than pitching generically, and tied the pitch to the prospect's real situation. (3) The rep was candid about limits and conceded weaknesses, such as no native connector, no housing-association reference, procurement risk and being a late third horse behind Tray. (4) The ask was small, low-pressure and not a demo: one email, a one-page note, a 30-minute call or a short note. The failed call had the opposite pattern. Alastair gave a generic pitch, got the practice count wrong, didn't ask questions, led with price ($1,800/month vs her $200-300 budget), and it was a poor fit.

answer.question: Which prospects seem most likely to purchase, based on the conversations?
answer.answer: Based on the transcripts, the strongest purchase signals come from Ember Financial (CALL-005), Juniper Cloud Tools (CALL-010) and Inkwell Learning (CALL-009), with Acme Logistics (CALL-001) a solid next tier. Ember is the clearest: it asked for sandbox access and a six-week pilot proposal, has a dated timeline driven by a remediation programme, and says the main gates (model risk, auditability) were addressed to the level a call allows. Its caveats are the Tray PoC's six-week head start and the cheaper 'document the scripts' alternative. Juniper has agreed a four-week evaluation starting Monday with go/no-go in September and four success criteria. The sponsor wants to proceed, but the engineer holds a practical veto and may favour building in-house. Inkwell is conditional on Darren's backward-looking analysis of 20 historical escalations; if the signal is present, Olivia wants a pilot, and the late-September decision date is real. Acme is 'interested enough to test it' and wants a sandbox with three real workflows, but must first win the internal Workato-expansion argument and cross the finance threshold. Lower or uncertain: BrightPath (CALL-002) is gated on a written BAA position, with no production before Q4. DeltaWorks (CALL-004) wants architecture material first and expects production early next year. Harbor Legal (CALL-008) has a Q4 PoC and Q1 decision but doubts that the integration effort is proportionate. Cedar & Finch (CALL-003) is a 'considered maybe' with budget the biggest risk. Fable Media (CALL-006) is interested but price-sensitive, and the vendor made unverified claims on SSO and billing. Greenline (CALL-007) is early exploration with no decision this year. The cold calls are mostly poor prospects, except Beacon Housing Trust (CALL-018), which has a follow-up booked but faces procurement hurdles. Renewals were not assessed as prospects.
